rules.sourceContent: •Every production AKS cluster SHALL place application pods on user node pools, with at leastthree nodes in the system node pool and at least two nodes in each user node pool. Systempods are thereby isolated from application resource demands.•Every production AKS workload with more than one replica MUST define a pod disruptionbudget. The budget keeps node upgrades and other voluntary disruptions from removing toomany pods at once.•Stateful container workloads MUST store persistent data on volumes outside the container, andin a zone-redundant region the volumes SHOULD use zone-redundant storage.Health probes and self-healing•Every container in a production deployment MUST define startup, readiness, and livenessprobes. Without them the platform cannot restart failed containers or withhold traffic fromcontainers that are not ready.•Liveness probes MUST test only the health of the container itself and MUST NOT checkdownstream dependencies. A dependency outage would otherwise trigger needless restartsacross every replica.•Readiness probe and startup probe settings SHALL allow enough time for the slowest expectedinitialization. Probe thresholds that restart a slow-starting container prematurely MUST NOT beused.•Applications that call other services SHOULD use platform-level resiliency policies, such asContainer Apps retries, timeouts, and circuit breakers, in addition to application-level handling.Scaling and resource limits•Every production container app and Functions deployment SHALL use automatic horizontalscaling with explicit scale rules, such as HTTP concurrency, queue depth, or CPU and memorythresholds, rather than manual instance counts.•Autoscaling rules MUST be load tested before production release, and scale events SHALL belogged so scaling behavior can be reviewed.•Every container in production MUST declare CPU and memory requests and limits. Limitsprevent a single container from starving neighbors and allow usage to be tuned from monitoreddata.•Session or application state SHALL NOT be held only in the memory of a single computeinstance. State that must survive restarts or scale-out MUST live in an external store that scalesindependently.•Azure Functions that process queue or event triggers MUST be idempotent and MUST usebuilt-in retry policies for transient errors. Long-running, multi-step workflows SHOULD useDurable Functions.Image provenance and patching

rules.sourceContent: •Every case where encryption of a production data store is not applied SHALL have adocumented technical or business justification approved by the security owner.Hardening and patching•Every compute, data, and platform resource in a production workload SHALL be deployed froma hardened configuration that disables unused features, ports, accounts, and services.•Every virtual machine in a production workload SHALL receive operating-system securityupdates through an automated patching process, and critical updates MUST be applied within14 days of release.•Every container image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into theorganization's security operations triage process.•Every security alert rule SHALL have a named owner and MUST be reviewed at least annuallyfor relevance and false-positive rate.•Security log data for production workloads MUST be retained for at least 12 months, or longerwhere a compliance obligation requires it.Security testing and incident response•Every production workload SHALL undergo penetration testing at least annually and aftersignificant architectural change.

rules.sourceContent: •Every API exposed to external or cross-team consumers SHALL be published through an APIgateway, such as Azure API Management, rather than directly from the backend service. Thegateway applies authentication, rate limiting, and policy consistently.•API gateway policies for every production API MUST enforce request rate limits or quotas andMUST validate inbound requests against the published contract.Service-to-service communication•Every outbound call to a remote service or dependency MUST have an explicit timeout. Callswithout timeouts SHALL NOT be shipped, because blocked threads and connections canexhaust resources.•Every retry policy MUST apply only to transient faults, use exponential backoff with jitter, andenforce a maximum attempt count. Retries for non-transient errors SHALL NOT be attempted.•Retry logic SHALL be implemented at only one layer of a call chain. Lower layers MUST failfast so that nested retries do not multiply delays and load.•Every dependency call that can fail persistently MUST be wrapped by a circuit breaker withdocumented failure threshold, open duration, and half-open probe behavior. Retry logic MUSTstop when the circuit breaker reports the circuit is open.•Retried operations that are not naturally idempotent MUST carry an idempotency key orrequest identifier that the receiving service uses to discard duplicates.•Early retry failures SHOULD be logged as informational entries and the final exhausted retryMUST be logged as an error, so that operators are not flooded with alerts for recovered faults.•Each service MUST own its data store, and other services SHALL access that data onlythrough the owning service's API or published events. Shared databases betweenindependently deployed services SHALL NOT be used.•Service boundaries SHOULD align with business capabilities, and each service MUST beindependently deployable and versionable.•Application code SHOULD use the official Azure SDK client libraries and their built-in retry andauthentication support instead of hand-built REST calls to Azure services.Messaging•Every messaging consumer MUST be idempotent, because Azure Service Bus and AzureEvent Grid deliver at least once. Consumers SHOULD track processed message identifiers todetect duplicates.•Every Service Bus queue and subscription SHALL have a dead-letter queue policy and adocumented process for reviewing and reprocessing dead-lettered messages. Poisonmessages MUST NOT block healthy message processing.•Production Service Bus namespaces that need zone or regional redundancy SHALL use thePremium tier, with zone redundancy and Geo-Replication enabled. The design MUSTdocument how and when a secondary region is promoted.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. rules.sourceContent: Chapter 16 — Architecture Documentation,Decisions and ReviewIntentA workload's architecture is the sum of its decisions, and decisions that are not recorded areforgotten, re-debated or silently contradicted. Documentation that is owned, versioned andreviewed gives operators, auditors and incident responders a single source of truth. This chaptersets obligations for decision records, diagrams, inventories, threat models, reviews and riskacceptance.RequirementsArchitecture decision records•Every workload MUST maintain an architecture decision record (ADR) log that is started at thebeginning of the workload and kept for its entire lifetime.•The ADR log MUST contain a record for each architecturally significant decision, meaning eachdecision that affects structure, a key quality attribute, or that is hard to reverse.•Every ADR MUST follow one common template containing at least the problem context, theoptions considered, the decision outcome, the trade-offs accepted, and the status.•Every ADR MUST carry a status of Proposed, Accepted or Superseded, and SHOULD recordthe confidence level of the decision when confidence is low.•The ADR log SHALL be append-only, so that an accepted record MUST NOT be edited tochange its decision, and a changed decision MUST be recorded as a new ADR that links to therecord it supersedes.•An ADR that spans several phases (short-term, mid-term, long-term) MUST be split into onerecord per phase.•Brownfield workloads without an ADR log MUST create one and SHOULD reconstruct recordsfor known past decisions.Diagrams and workload documentation•The workload documentation MUST include a context diagram, a logical or componentdiagram, and a deployment or network topology diagram, each showing the trust boundaries.•Each diagram MUST identify its subject, its version or date, and its owner, and every diagramSHALL use a consistent notation with a legend.•The documentation MUST describe the data flows for each category of sensitive data, includingwhere data is stored, processed and transmitted.•The documentation MUST list the workload's reliability targets (SLOs, RTO and RPO), andSHALL link each to the design elements that support it.

rules.sourceContent: •Every case where encryption of a production data store is not applied SHALL have adocumented technical or business justification approved by the security owner.Hardening and patching•Every compute, data, and platform resource in a production workload SHALL be deployed froma hardened configuration that disables unused features, ports, accounts, and services.•Every virtual machine in a production workload SHALL receive operating-system securityupdates through an automated patching process, and critical updates MUST be applied within14 days of release.•Every container image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into theorganization's security operations triage process.•Every security alert rule SHALL have a named owner and MUST be reviewed at least annuallyfor relevance and false-positive rate.•Security log data for production workloads MUST be retained for at least 12 months, or longerwhere a compliance obligation requires it.Security testing and incident response•Every production workload SHALL undergo penetration testing at least annually and aftersignificant architectural change.

rules.sourceContent: •The team MUST record the source, version, licence terms and intended use of every model in amodel inventory and MUST confirm that the licence permits the intended commercial use.•The workload MUST keep prompts, system messages and model configuration in versioncontrol and SHALL deploy them through a controlled release process, so that telemetry can becorrelated with a specific prompt version.•The design MUST plan for model deprecation by recording the retirement date of each hostedmodel version and by providing a tested fallback model or migration path before that date.•Training, fine-tuning and grounding data MUST have a documented owner, classification,lineage and retention period, and personal or confidential data SHALL NOT be used for trainingunless the legal basis is recorded.•Retrieval over grounding data MUST enforce the end user's authorization, by passing user ortenant identity to the retrieval layer so results are security-trimmed, and AI components MUSTNOT read data stores directly.Evaluation and monitoring•The team MUST evaluate each model and prompt change against a versioned test dataset forgroundedness, relevance, safety and accuracy before release, and SHALL block release whenresults fall below defined thresholds.•The workload MUST include red-team or adversarial testing of the AI feature before initialproduction release and after any change of model, grounding source or system prompt.•The production workload MUST monitor model quality indicators (accuracy drift, inferencelatency, confidence scores and input data distribution) and SHALL alert when a definedthreshold is breached.•The workload MUST log prompts, completions and tool calls with user identity and promptversion for audit, and the log retention and redaction rules SHALL be documented for anypersonal data they contain.Identity, secrets and network•Services calling Azure OpenAI, Azure AI services or Azure Machine Learning endpoints MUSTauthenticate with managed identities or Microsoft Entra ID, and API keys MUST NOT beembedded in code or configuration files.•Where API keys cannot be avoided, the workload MUST store them in Azure Key Vault andSHALL rotate them at least every 90 days.•Production AI endpoints and grounding data stores SHOULD be reachable only through privateendpoints, and public network access MUST be disabled unless a documented exceptionexists.•Agents and tools MUST run with the least-privilege identity needed for their actions, and anytool that changes state SHALL require explicit authorization checks independent of the model'soutput.Cost and capacity

rules.sourceContent: •Every case where encryption of a production data store is not applied SHALL have adocumented technical or business justification approved by the security owner.Hardening and patching•Every compute, data, and platform resource in a production workload SHALL be deployed froma hardened configuration that disables unused features, ports, accounts, and services.•Every virtual machine in a production workload SHALL receive operating-system securityupdates through an automated patching process, and critical updates MUST be applied within14 days of release.•Every container image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into theorganization's security operations triage process.•Every security alert rule SHALL have a named owner and MUST be reviewed at least annuallyfor relevance and false-positive rate.•Security log data for production workloads MUST be retained for at least 12 months, or longerwhere a compliance obligation requires it.Security testing and incident response•Every production workload SHALL undergo penetration testing at least annually and aftersignificant architectural change.

rules.sourceContent: •Capacity planning MUST be performed before any predicted change in usage, such asseasonal peaks, product launches, or marketing events. It SHALL be based on historicalutilization data, or on pilots and expert estimates when no history exists.•The capacity plan for every production workload MUST be reviewed at least annually andMUST include a demand forecast, identified bottleneck components, and the resource quotasand regional capacity that need to be reserved or increased.•Subscription quotas and regional capacity limits for every service that a critical workloaddepends on MUST be verified in both primary and secondary regions before launch.Caching•Cache use SHALL be limited to data that is read frequently and changed infrequently. A cacheMUST NOT be the authoritative store of critical data, and the system of record MUST remain apersistent data store.•Every cached item MUST have an explicit expiration policy, and the design MUST describehow stale or inconsistent cached data is detected or invalidated.•Applications MUST continue to operate, with degraded performance if necessary, when thecache is unavailable. Cache seeding of a large cache SHOULD be staged to avoid overloadingthe data store at startup.•Workloads with multiple application instances that need a consistent view of cached dataSHOULD use a shared cache, such as Azure Managed Redis, instead of per-instancein-memory caches.Sources•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/reliability/disaster-recovery•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/reliability/testing-strategy•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/performance-efficiency/performance-test•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/performance-efficiency/capacity-planning•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/architecture/best-practices/caching

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 7 — Operational Excellence, CI/CD andInfrastructure as CodeIntentReliable operations depend on repeatable, automated, and reviewed change. This chapter setsobligations for infrastructure as code, pipelines, environment separation, deployment safety,secret handling, documentation, and change management. Following them reduces human error,configuration drift, and the blast radius of faulty releases.RequirementsInfrastructure as code•All infrastructure and configuration changes to production environments MUST be madethrough infrastructure as code and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual changes in theAzure portal SHALL NOT be made to production except during a documented emergency.•Infrastructure as code SHOULD use a declarative approach, such as Bicep or Terraform, inpreference to imperative scripts.•Infrastructure as code definitions MUST be stored in version control and reviewed through pullrequests before they are merged to the deployment branch.•Infrastructure as code MUST be organized into modules with defined inputs and outputs, andmodule versions SHALL be pinned.•Deployment code SHALL NOT reference the latest version of a tool, API, provider, or module.Every such reference MUST name an explicitly tested version.•The organization SHOULD maintain a style guide that standardizes the infrastructure as codetools, naming, and structure used by all teams.•Configuration drift between deployed resources and their code definitions MUST be detectedon a recurring schedule, and detected drift SHALL be corrected through code rather thanmanual edits.Environments•Every workload MUST have at least one nonproduction environment that matches production intopology and configuration, so that releases are validated before they reach production.•All environments of a workload SHALL be created from the same infrastructure as codedefinitions, differing only by parameter values.•Production and nonproduction environments MUST be isolated by separate subscriptions orresource groups, with separate identities and access assignments.CI/CD pipelines•Every production deployment MUST be performed by an automated pipeline, and the pipelinedefinition SHALL be stored in version control.

Pipelines MUST retrieve secrets at run time from a secret store such asAzure Key Vault or the pipeline platform's protected secret storage.•Source repositories MUST have secret scanning enabled, and any credential detected in arepository MUST be rotated immediately.•Pipeline service connections and tokens MUST have a defined owner and SHALL be reviewedat least annually.Branching and code review•The default branch of every workload repository MUST be protected so that direct pushes arerejected and changes require a reviewed pull request with passing status checks.•Teams SHOULD use short-lived branches and integrate to the default branch at least daily, sothat changes remain small and incremental.Deployment safety•Every deployment, including code, infrastructure, feature flag, and configuration changes,MUST follow the same standardized, automated process. rules.sourceContent: Chapter 9 — Compute, Containers and HostingIntentCompute and container hosting decisions determine how a workload scales, recovers, and ispatched for its entire life. Choosing the wrong platform, running too few instances, or shippingunverified images creates availability and security debt that is expensive to reverse. This chaptersets baseline obligations for selecting hosting platforms and for operating Azure Container Apps,Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS), Azure App Service and Azure Functions in production.RequirementsHosting platform selection•Every workload design document SHALL record the compute platform decision, including thealternatives considered, by reference to the Azure compute decision tree. This makes therationale for the platform reviewable.•A design that selects Azure Container Apps express for a production workload MUSTdocument that the workload does not need fine-grained control over compute, networking, orcold-start behavior. Workloads that need that control SHOULD use Container Apps with aworkload profiles environment.•A design that selects AKS for a new production workload SHOULD use AKS Automatic andMUST document the specific requirement, such as Windows node pools or bring-your-ownCNI, that justifies AKS Standard when AKS Standard is chosen.•Every hosting design MUST state which team owns each part of the platform, with the platformteam owning cluster or plan configuration and the application team owning manifests,application identity, and workload monitoring.•Unrelated workloads SHOULD run in separate AKS clusters. A shared AKS cluster MUST usenamespaces, dedicated node pools, and network policies to enforce isolation between theworkloads it hosts.Redundancy and availability•Every production Container Apps app exposed through HTTP or TCP ingress SHALL run atleast three replicas. Apps that are sensitive to cold starts MUST configure a minimum numberof always-ready replicas.•Every production compute deployment in a region that offers availability zones MUST enablezone redundancy for Container Apps environments, AKS node pools, and App Service plans.This keeps a single zone failure from taking the workload down.•A production App Service app SHALL run on at least two instances. A single-instancedeployment is a single point of failure.•Compute for a critical workload MUST be deployed to at least two Azure regions, with AzureFront Door or Azure Traffic Manager routing traffic between them.

rules.sourceContent: •The number of Azure Policy assignments at the tenant root management group SHALL be keptto a minimum. Root-scope assignments MUST be limited to controls that apply to everysubscription.•Policy definitions SHALL be written once and reused through initiatives at multiple inheritedscopes, and all definitions and assignments MUST be managed as code in source control.•Every new policy MUST be rolled out first in audit mode or at a limited scope and reviewed forimpact before its effect changes to deny or enforce.•Every non-compliant resource that Azure Policy reports MUST be remediated or covered by anapproved exception, and remediation tasks SHOULD be used to correct existing resourcesautomatically.Access governance•Workload team members SHALL NOT receive RBAC role assignments at management groupscope. Their roles MUST be assigned at the subscription or resource group scope that theyneed.•Standing RBAC assignments at management group scope for platform teams SHOULD beeligible, not permanent, through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management with activationlimited to the time needed.•Every RBAC role assignment SHALL follow least privilege, and assignments MUST be made togroups rather than to individual users where practical.•Access to every production subscription MUST be reviewed at least every six months, andassignments that are no longer needed MUST be removed.Naming and tagging•The organization SHALL define and publish one resource naming convention that specifies theordering of components such as resource type, workload, environment, region, and instancenumber. Every Azure resource MUST follow it.•Resource names MUST NOT contain sensitive, personal, or confidential information, becausenames and tags are visible to many services and are not treated as customer data.•Every Azure resource that supports tags MUST carry a defined mandatory tag set that coversat least workload, environment, owner, and cost center. Azure Policy MUST enforce or appendthese tags.•Tag names SHALL use consistent lowercase keys and a controlled vocabulary of values,because tag values are case-sensitive. Tags SHALL NOT hold secrets or sensitive data.Compliance, audit and exceptions•The organization MUST map each applicable regulatory or contractual obligation, such asHIPAA, PCI-DSS, or SOC 2, to specific Azure Policy initiatives or controls, and MUST reviewthe mapping at least annually.

rules.sourceContent: •Tag inheritance SHOULD be enabled in Cost Management, so that costs of resources areattributed to the tags set at the subscription or resource group level.•Shared platform costs MUST be allocated to consuming workloads by a documented allocationrule rather than being left unassigned.Showback and chargeback•The organization MUST produce showback reports at least monthly that show each businessunit or workload owner the cost it incurred.•Where chargeback is practiced, the allocation method MUST be documented, approved byfinance, and applied consistently across all consuming teams.Guardrails•Spending guardrails MUST be implemented through platform automation, such as Azure Policyrestrictions on permitted SKUs and regions, rather than by manual review alone.•Resource creation rights in production MUST be restricted to approved roles or pipelines, sothat unmanaged resources cannot generate unbudgeted cost.•Nonproduction environments SHOULD use lower-cost SKUs than production and SHALL beshut down or scaled to zero outside working hours when they are not needed.Rightsizing and lifecycle•Resource sizes MUST be reviewed against measured utilization at least quarterly, andresources whose sustained utilization is below the documented threshold SHALL be downsizedor removed.•Orphaned resources, such as unattached disks, unused public IP addresses, and idlegateways, MUST be identified and deleted on a recurring schedule.•Data in Azure Storage SHOULD be moved to cooler access tiers through lifecycle managementpolicies when its access frequency declines.•Log and telemetry volume MUST be reviewed periodically, and low-value data SHOULD befiltered, sampled, or moved to a lower-cost tier.Reservations, savings plans and licensing•Workloads with steady, predictable usage SHOULD be covered by Azure Reservations orAzure savings plans, with coverage reviewed at least annually.•Commitments MUST NOT be purchased until at least one representative period of utilizationdata supports the commitment size.•Existing eligible licenses SHOULD be applied through Azure Hybrid Benefit, and theorganization MUST track license entitlements to avoid paying twice.•Development and test workloads SHOULD use Azure Dev/Test pricing where theorganization's agreement permits.Autoscaling

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 5 — Data, Storage and PrivacyIntentData is the asset most likely to cause lasting harm when it is exposed, altered, or lost. This chaptersets obligations for classifying data, protecting it at rest and in transit, managing encryption keys,and keeping it recoverable. Applying these obligations consistently lets each data store receiveprotection proportionate to the sensitivity of its contents.RequirementsData classification and ownership•Every workload data store and every system that processes workload data SHALL carry adocumented sensitivity classification drawn from the organization's classification taxonomy.Classification drives the protection level that is applied to the data.•The design document MUST record the location of every store that holds classified data,including copies in backups, caches, analytics stores, and nonproduction environments. Datathat is not located cannot be protected.•Each data store MUST have a named owner who is accountable for its classification, accessapprovals, and retention. Ownership prevents orphaned data from accumulating withoutcontrols.•Automated data discovery tooling SHOULD be used to suggest classifications, and a humanreview of the suggested classifications MUST occur before they are accepted. Tooling alonedoes not replace team accountability.•Production data classified as confidential or restricted SHALL NOT be copied into developmentor test environments unless it has first been masked or anonymized.Encryption at rest•All data at rest in production storage, including databases, storage accounts, managed disks,and backups, MUST be encrypted. Platform-native encryption SHOULD be used instead ofcustom encryption.•Teams SHALL NOT disable platform-provided encryption in order to substitute a customimplementation unless a documented evaluation shows the platform capability cannot meet astated requirement.•Any custom cryptography that is permitted MUST use industry-standard algorithms and thecryptography APIs of the operating system or runtime rather than bespoke or nonplatformlibraries.•Data classified as confidential or restricted SHOULD be protected with customer-managedkeys when regulation or policy requires the organization to control key rotation, revocation, orthe ability to render data undecryptable.•Any data store that is not encrypted at rest MUST have a documented, approved exception thatstates the technical or business reason.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 5 — Data, Storage and PrivacyIntentData is the asset most likely to cause lasting harm when it is exposed, altered, or lost. This chaptersets obligations for classifying data, protecting it at rest and in transit, managing encryption keys,and keeping it recoverable. Applying these obligations consistently lets each data store receiveprotection proportionate to the sensitivity of its contents.RequirementsData classification and ownership•Every workload data store and every system that processes workload data SHALL carry adocumented sensitivity classification drawn from the organization's classification taxonomy.Classification drives the protection level that is applied to the data.•The design document MUST record the location of every store that holds classified data,including copies in backups, caches, analytics stores, and nonproduction environments. Datathat is not located cannot be protected.•Each data store MUST have a named owner who is accountable for its classification, accessapprovals, and retention. Ownership prevents orphaned data from accumulating withoutcontrols.•Automated data discovery tooling SHOULD be used to suggest classifications, and a humanreview of the suggested classifications MUST occur before they are accepted. Tooling alonedoes not replace team accountability.•Production data classified as confidential or restricted SHALL NOT be copied into developmentor test environments unless it has first been masked or anonymized.Encryption at rest•All data at rest in production storage, including databases, storage accounts, managed disks,and backups, MUST be encrypted. Platform-native encryption SHOULD be used instead ofcustom encryption.•Teams SHALL NOT disable platform-provided encryption in order to substitute a customimplementation unless a documented evaluation shows the platform capability cannot meet astated requirement.•Any custom cryptography that is permitted MUST use industry-standard algorithms and thecryptography APIs of the operating system or runtime rather than bespoke or nonplatformlibraries.•Data classified as confidential or restricted SHOULD be protected with customer-managedkeys when regulation or policy requires the organization to control key rotation, revocation, orthe ability to render data undecryptable.•Any data store that is not encrypted at rest MUST have a documented, approved exception thatstates the technical or business reason.

rules.sourceContent: •The team MUST record the source, version, licence terms and intended use of every model in amodel inventory and MUST confirm that the licence permits the intended commercial use.•The workload MUST keep prompts, system messages and model configuration in versioncontrol and SHALL deploy them through a controlled release process, so that telemetry can becorrelated with a specific prompt version.•The design MUST plan for model deprecation by recording the retirement date of each hostedmodel version and by providing a tested fallback model or migration path before that date.•Training, fine-tuning and grounding data MUST have a documented owner, classification,lineage and retention period, and personal or confidential data SHALL NOT be used for trainingunless the legal basis is recorded.•Retrieval over grounding data MUST enforce the end user's authorization, by passing user ortenant identity to the retrieval layer so results are security-trimmed, and AI components MUSTNOT read data stores directly.Evaluation and monitoring•The team MUST evaluate each model and prompt change against a versioned test dataset forgroundedness, relevance, safety and accuracy before release, and SHALL block release whenresults fall below defined thresholds.•The workload MUST include red-team or adversarial testing of the AI feature before initialproduction release and after any change of model, grounding source or system prompt.•The production workload MUST monitor model quality indicators (accuracy drift, inferencelatency, confidence scores and input data distribution) and SHALL alert when a definedthreshold is breached.•The workload MUST log prompts, completions and tool calls with user identity and promptversion for audit, and the log retention and redaction rules SHALL be documented for anypersonal data they contain.Identity, secrets and network•Services calling Azure OpenAI, Azure AI services or Azure Machine Learning endpoints MUSTauthenticate with managed identities or Microsoft Entra ID, and API keys MUST NOT beembedded in code or configuration files.•Where API keys cannot be avoided, the workload MUST store them in Azure Key Vault andSHALL rotate them at least every 90 days.•Production AI endpoints and grounding data stores SHOULD be reachable only through privateendpoints, and public network access MUST be disabled unless a documented exceptionexists.•Agents and tools MUST run with the least-privilege identity needed for their actions, and anytool that changes state SHALL require explicit authorization checks independent of the model'soutput.Cost and capacity

rules.sourceContent: Region and placement•The design MUST document the selection of each deployment region and SHALL weighcarbon intensity, latency, data residency and service availability.•Batch, training and other delay-tolerant workloads SHOULD be scheduled in lower-carbonregions or time windows when no latency or residency constraint prevents it.•The design MUST NOT replicate workloads across more regions than the documentedavailability objective requires, and every extra region SHALL be justified by a reliability orresidency requirement.•Components that exchange large volumes of data SHOULD be co-located in the same regionand zone to avoid unnecessary data transfer.Efficient application and data design•The design SHOULD use caching, asynchronous and event-driven processing, and efficientdata access patterns to reduce repeated computation, and the architecture document MUSTidentify the main hot paths for which this was considered.•The workload MUST set a documented retention period for every data store, log and backup,and automated lifecycle rules SHALL delete or archive data when that period ends.•Data that is rarely accessed MUST be moved to cooler or archive storage tiers by lifecyclepolicy rather than kept in the hot tier.•The workload MUST NOT replicate data to additional copies, regions or tiers beyond what itsrecovery objectives require.•Telemetry collection MUST be limited to data with a defined operational purpose, with loglevels, sampling and retention set per environment, and verbose logging SHALL NOT beenabled by default in production.•Container images and build artifacts MUST be retained under a defined cleanup policy, and theCI/CD pipeline SHOULD avoid redundant full builds and test runs.AI and data-intensive workloads•AI workloads SHOULD use the smallest model and the lowest-precision compute that satisfythe documented quality target, and the selection rationale MUST be recorded.•GPU and other accelerator resources MUST be released or scaled down when training orinference jobs complete, and idle accelerator time SHALL be reported at least monthly.Sources•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/sustainability/overview•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/sustainability/sustainability-design-principles•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/ai/application-design

rules.sourceContent: Region and placement•The design MUST document the selection of each deployment region and SHALL weighcarbon intensity, latency, data residency and service availability.•Batch, training and other delay-tolerant workloads SHOULD be scheduled in lower-carbonregions or time windows when no latency or residency constraint prevents it.•The design MUST NOT replicate workloads across more regions than the documentedavailability objective requires, and every extra region SHALL be justified by a reliability orresidency requirement.•Components that exchange large volumes of data SHOULD be co-located in the same regionand zone to avoid unnecessary data transfer.Efficient application and data design•The design SHOULD use caching, asynchronous and event-driven processing, and efficientdata access patterns to reduce repeated computation, and the architecture document MUSTidentify the main hot paths for which this was considered.•The workload MUST set a documented retention period for every data store, log and backup,and automated lifecycle rules SHALL delete or archive data when that period ends.•Data that is rarely accessed MUST be moved to cooler or archive storage tiers by lifecyclepolicy rather than kept in the hot tier.•The workload MUST NOT replicate data to additional copies, regions or tiers beyond what itsrecovery objectives require.•Telemetry collection MUST be limited to data with a defined operational purpose, with loglevels, sampling and retention set per environment, and verbose logging SHALL NOT beenabled by default in production.•Container images and build artifacts MUST be retained under a defined cleanup policy, and theCI/CD pipeline SHOULD avoid redundant full builds and test runs.AI and data-intensive workloads•AI workloads SHOULD use the smallest model and the lowest-precision compute that satisfythe documented quality target, and the selection rationale MUST be recorded.•GPU and other accelerator resources MUST be released or scaled down when training orinference jobs complete, and idle accelerator time SHALL be reported at least monthly.Sources•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/sustainability/overview•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/sustainability/sustainability-design-principles•https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/well-architected/ai/application-design

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 7 — Operational Excellence, CI/CD andInfrastructure as CodeIntentReliable operations depend on repeatable, automated, and reviewed change. This chapter setsobligations for infrastructure as code, pipelines, environment separation, deployment safety,secret handling, documentation, and change management. Following them reduces human error,configuration drift, and the blast radius of faulty releases.RequirementsInfrastructure as code•All infrastructure and configuration changes to production environments MUST be madethrough infrastructure as code and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual changes in theAzure portal SHALL NOT be made to production except during a documented emergency.•Infrastructure as code SHOULD use a declarative approach, such as Bicep or Terraform, inpreference to imperative scripts.•Infrastructure as code definitions MUST be stored in version control and reviewed through pullrequests before they are merged to the deployment branch.•Infrastructure as code MUST be organized into modules with defined inputs and outputs, andmodule versions SHALL be pinned.•Deployment code SHALL NOT reference the latest version of a tool, API, provider, or module.Every such reference MUST name an explicitly tested version.•The organization SHOULD maintain a style guide that standardizes the infrastructure as codetools, naming, and structure used by all teams.•Configuration drift between deployed resources and their code definitions MUST be detectedon a recurring schedule, and detected drift SHALL be corrected through code rather thanmanual edits.Environments•Every workload MUST have at least one nonproduction environment that matches production intopology and configuration, so that releases are validated before they reach production.•All environments of a workload SHALL be created from the same infrastructure as codedefinitions, differing only by parameter values.•Production and nonproduction environments MUST be isolated by separate subscriptions orresource groups, with separate identities and access assignments.CI/CD pipelines•Every production deployment MUST be performed by an automated pipeline, and the pipelinedefinition SHALL be stored in version control.

use.•The workload MUST keep prompts, system messages and model configuration in versioncontrol and SHALL deploy them through a controlled release process, so that telemetry can becorrelated with a specific prompt version.•The design MUST plan for model deprecation by recording the retirement date of each hostedmodel version and by providing a tested fallback model or migration path before that date.•Training, fine-tuning and grounding data MUST have a documented owner, classification,lineage and retention period, and personal or confidential data SHALL NOT be used for trainingunless the rules.sourceContent: Chapter 7 — Operational Excellence, CI/CD andInfrastructure as CodeIntentReliable operations depend on repeatable, automated, and reviewed change. This chapter setsobligations for infrastructure as code, pipelines, environment separation, deployment safety,secret handling, documentation, and change management. Following them reduces human error,configuration drift, and the blast radius of faulty releases.RequirementsInfrastructure as code•All infrastructure and configuration changes to production environments MUST be madethrough infrastructure as code and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual changes in theAzure portal SHALL NOT be made to production except during a documented emergency.•Infrastructure as code SHOULD use a declarative approach, such as Bicep or Terraform, inpreference to imperative scripts.•Infrastructure as code definitions MUST be stored in version control and reviewed through pullrequests before they are merged to the deployment branch.•Infrastructure as code MUST be organized into modules with defined inputs and outputs, andmodule versions SHALL be pinned.•Deployment code SHALL NOT reference the latest version of a tool, API, provider, or module.Every such reference MUST name an explicitly tested version.•The organization SHOULD maintain a style guide that standardizes the infrastructure as codetools, naming, and structure used by all teams.•Configuration drift between deployed resources and their code definitions MUST be detectedon a recurring schedule, and detected drift SHALL be corrected through code rather thanmanual edits.Environments•Every workload MUST have at least one nonproduction environment that matches production intopology and configuration, so that releases are validated before they reach production.•All environments of a workload SHALL be created from the same infrastructure as codedefinitions, differing only by parameter values.•Production and nonproduction environments MUST be isolated by separate subscriptions orresource groups, with separate identities and access assignments.CI/CD pipelines•Every production deployment MUST be performed by an automated pipeline, and the pipelinedefinition SHALL be stored in version control.

Following them reduces human error,configuration drift, and the blast radius of faulty releases.RequirementsInfrastructure as code•All infrastructure and configuration changes to production environments MUST be madethrough infrastructure as code and deployed through a CI/CD pipeline. Manual changes in theAzure portal SHALL NOT be made to production except during a documented emergency.•Infrastructure as code SHOULD use a declarative approach, such as Bicep or Terraform, inpreference to imperative scripts.•Infrastructure as code definitions MUST be stored in version control and reviewed through pullrequests before they are merged to the deployment branch.•Infrastructure as code MUST be organized into modules with defined inputs and outputs, andmodule versions SHALL be pinned.•Deployment code SHALL NOT reference the latest version of a tool, API, provider, or module.Every such reference MUST name an explicitly tested version.•The organization SHOULD maintain a style guide that standardizes the infrastructure as codetools, naming, and structure used by all teams.•Configuration drift between deployed resources and their code definitions MUST be detectedon a recurring schedule, and detected drift SHALL be corrected through code rather thanmanual edits.Environments•Every workload MUST have at least one nonproduction environment that matches production intopology and configuration, so that releases are validated before they reach production.•All environments of a workload SHALL be created from the same infrastructure as codedefinitions, differing only by parameter values.•Production and nonproduction environments MUST be isolated by separate subscriptions orresource groups, with separate identities and access assignments.CI/CD pipelines•Every production deployment MUST be performed by an automated pipeline, and the pipelinedefinition SHALL be stored in version control.

rules.sourceContent: •Every case where encryption of a production data store is not applied SHALL have adocumented technical or business justification approved by the security owner.Hardening and patching•Every compute, data, and platform resource in a production workload SHALL be deployed froma hardened configuration that disables unused features, ports, accounts, and services.•Every virtual machine in a production workload SHALL receive operating-system securityupdates through an automated patching process, and critical updates MUST be applied within14 days of release.•Every container image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into theorganization's security operations triage process.•Every security alert rule SHALL have a named owner and MUST be reviewed at least annuallyfor relevance and false-positive rate.•Security log data for production workloads MUST be retained for at least 12 months, or longerwhere a compliance obligation requires it.Security testing and incident response•Every production workload SHALL undergo penetration testing at least annually and aftersignificant architectural change.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 3 — Identity and Access ManagementIntentIdentity is the primary security perimeter for cloud workloads, covering people, services, andanonymous callers alike. This chapter requires one trusted identity provider, strong and conditionalauthentication, least-privilege authorization, and auditable access. Together these controls ensurethat every action is attributable and limited to what is necessary.RequirementsIdentity provider and authentication•Every production workload SHALL authenticate all human and system identities throughMicrosoft Entra ID or another centrally managed identity provider approved by the organization.•Production workloads MUST NOT implement custom user stores or custom authenticationmechanisms in place of the approved identity provider.•Every production workload SHALL use modern authentication and authorization protocols suchas OpenID Connect and OAuth 2.0, and legacy protocols such as basic authentication MUSTNOT be enabled.•Every production workload SHALL document both outside-in access (users and operatorsreaching the workload) and inside-out access (the workload reaching other resources), togetherwith the identity used for each flow.•Every production workload SHALL define which resources are accessed anonymously, andanonymous access MUST be limited to resources that are intended to be public.Multifactor and conditional access•Every interactive human account with access to production resources SHALL be protected bymultifactor authentication.•Every administrative role assignment on production resources MUST require phishing-resistantor conditional-access-enforced multifactor authentication.•Production access policies SHOULD apply Conditional Access that evaluates user risk, sign-inrisk, device compliance, and location before granting access.•Legacy authentication protocols SHALL be blocked by Conditional Access policy for allaccounts with access to production resources.•Break-glass emergency accounts SHALL be limited to at most two per tenant, MUST beexcluded from normal Conditional Access dependencies only by documented design, andSHALL have every sign-in alerted.Authorization and least privilege•Every role assignment on production Azure resources SHALL follow least privilege and bescoped to the narrowest resource, resource group, or subscription that meets the need.

rules.sourceContent: •Every case where encryption of a production data store is not applied SHALL have adocumented technical or business justification approved by the security owner.Hardening and patching•Every compute, data, and platform resource in a production workload SHALL be deployed froma hardened configuration that disables unused features, ports, accounts, and services.•Every virtual machine in a production workload SHALL receive operating-system securityupdates through an automated patching process, and critical updates MUST be applied within14 days of release.•Every container image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into theorganization's security operations triage process.•Every security alert rule SHALL have a named owner and MUST be reviewed at least annuallyfor relevance and false-positive rate.•Security log data for production workloads MUST be retained for at least 12 months, or longerwhere a compliance obligation requires it.Security testing and incident response•Every production workload SHALL undergo penetration testing at least annually and aftersignificant architectural change.

rules.sourceContent: •Workspace-based Application Insights resources SHOULD be used so that application andinfrastructure telemetry can be queried together.•Access to log workspaces MUST be controlled by role-based access control, and workspacesholding security or audit data SHALL be restricted to authorized personnel.Retention•The retention period for each log category MUST be defined in the design document andSHALL satisfy the longest applicable regulatory or organizational requirement.•Audit and security logs SHOULD be kept for at least one year, using archive or long-termstorage tiers for the period beyond interactive retention to control cost.•Log data MUST be protected from alteration and deletion for the duration of its retention period.Distributed tracing and sampling•Every request that crosses a service boundary MUST propagate a correlation identifier, usingthe W3C Trace Context standard, so that a transaction can be traced end to end.•Services in a distributed system SHALL emit trace spans for all inbound requests and outbounddependency calls.•Sampling, when used for traces or telemetry in production, MUST preserve all failed requestsand all exceptions. The sampling rate SHALL be documented, and sampling decisions MUSTbe consistent across the services in a single transaction.Alerting•Every alert MUST have a named owning team, a severity, and a linked runbook or responseprocedure. Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. Alerting MUST include at least one notification path that is independent of themonitored workload.•Alert rules SHALL be reviewed at least quarterly, and rules that are noisy or never actionableMUST be tuned or removed.SLIs, SLOs and error budgets•Every production service MUST define at least one service-level indicator for availability andone for latency, each with a documented measurement method.•Every production service MUST have a service-level objective for each indicator, agreed withthe service's business owner, with a stated measurement window.•Teams SHOULD track an error budget derived from each objective and MUST define theactions taken, such as pausing feature releases, when the budget is exhausted.Incident response

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 6 — Monitoring, Logging, Tracing and SREIntentTeams can only operate what they can observe. This chapter sets obligations for telemetry design,log handling, alerting, service-level objectives, distributed tracing, and incident response so thatdegradation is detected early and diagnosed quickly. It treats the monitoring stack as a first-classpart of the workload rather than an afterthought.RequirementsHealth model and telemetry design•Every workload SHALL define a health model that lists its health indicators, key performanceindicators, and the metrics that feed them. Telemetry collection MUST be derived from thatmodel.•The health model MUST map user flows and system flows to the resources that support them,so that degradation in a dependency is visible at the level where business impact occurs.•Workload components MUST emit structured telemetry that uses a consistent schema andincludes the source component, a timestamp, and a correlation identifier.•Applications SHOULD use a configurable logging framework that is decoupled from anyspecific monitoring backend, so the backend can change without code changes.Logging practices•Logs MUST NOT contain secrets, credentials, or unmasked personal or sensitive data.Applications SHALL scrub such values before writing log entries.•Telemetry MUST be classified by operational concern, such as audit, security, debugging, andperformance, so that access controls and retention can be applied per category.•Workload business data SHALL NOT be stored in telemetry stores. Telemetry and workloaddata MUST be kept separate.•Production logging verbosity SHOULD be lower than development verbosity and MUST beadjustable at runtime or by configuration without redeployment.•Telemetry emission MUST be non-blocking and MUST NOT cause the application to fail whenthe monitoring backend is unavailable. The only exception is critical audit logging that isrequired by regulation.Azure Monitor and Application Insights•Every production Azure resource MUST send platform logs and metrics to a Log Analyticsworkspace through diagnostic settings. Diagnostic settings SHOULD be deployed by AzurePolicy so that new resources are covered automatically.•Every production application MUST be instrumented with Application Insights, or anOpenTelemetry-based equivalent that exports to Azure Monitor, so that requests,dependencies, exceptions, and performance counters are captured.

rules.sourceContent: •The design MUST test tenant isolation continuously, including automated cross-tenant accesstests in the release pipeline for every production release.•Tenants with stricter isolation or compliance needs SHOULD be offered a dedicateddeployment or dedicated data store, and the document MUST describe how those tenants arerouted to it.•The design MUST document the data residency location of each tenant's data and SHALLensure that tenant data, backups and replicas remain within the region or geography the tenantcontracted for.•The solution MUST support per-tenant encryption key options (for example customer-managedkeys in Azure Key Vault) wherever tenants have contractual requirements for key control, andthe design SHALL document which tiers receive them.•Custom domain handling MUST include a process for removing DNS records when a tenant isoffboarded, so that dangling DNS entries cannot be used for subdomain takeover.Tenant-aware identity and request mapping•The identity design MUST map every authenticated request to exactly one tenant by using averifiable claim in the token, a trusted lookup, or another documented mechanism, and MUSTNOT management operations.•Operator and support access to tenant data MUST be limited to approved, time-bound andlogged sessions.Noisy neighbour and fairness•The design MUST include resource governance that prevents a single tenant from exhaustingshared capacity, using per-tenant quotas, rate limits or throttling that return a defined error tothe caller.•The platform MUST monitor resource consumption per tenant as well as in aggregate, andSHALL alert on per-tenant usage spikes before shared capacity is exhausted.•The design SHOULD offer higher-isolation tiers (reserved throughput, premium service tiers ordedicated instances) for tenants whose workload would otherwise threaten shared capacity.•The team MUST define service-level objectives for the solution based on tenant rules.sourceContent: •Every API exposed to external or cross-team consumers SHALL be published through an APIgateway, such as Azure API Management, rather than directly from the backend service. Thegateway applies authentication, rate limiting, and policy consistently.•API gateway policies for every production API MUST enforce request rate limits or quotas andMUST validate inbound requests against the published contract.Service-to-service communication•Every outbound call to a remote service or dependency MUST have an explicit timeout. Callswithout timeouts SHALL NOT be shipped, because blocked threads and connections canexhaust resources.•Every retry policy MUST apply only to transient faults, use exponential backoff with jitter, andenforce a maximum attempt count. Retries for non-transient errors SHALL NOT be attempted.•Retry logic SHALL be implemented at only one layer of a call chain. Lower layers MUST failfast so that nested retries do not multiply delays and load.•Every dependency call that can fail persistently MUST be wrapped by a circuit breaker withdocumented failure threshold, open duration, and half-open probe behavior. Retry logic MUSTstop when the circuit breaker reports the circuit is open.•Retried operations that are not naturally idempotent MUST carry an idempotency key orrequest identifier that the receiving service uses to discard duplicates.•Early retry failures SHOULD be logged as informational entries and the final exhausted retryMUST be logged as an error, so that operators are not flooded with alerts for recovered faults.•Each service MUST own its data store, and other services SHALL access that data onlythrough the owning service's API or published events. Shared databases betweenindependently deployed services SHALL NOT be used.•Service boundaries SHOULD align with business capabilities, and each service MUST beindependently deployable and versionable.•Application code SHOULD use the official Azure SDK client libraries and their built-in retry andauthentication support instead of hand-built REST calls to Azure services.Messaging•Every messaging consumer MUST be idempotent, because Azure Service Bus and AzureEvent Grid deliver at least once. Consumers SHOULD track processed message identifiers todetect duplicates.•Every Service Bus queue and subscription SHALL have a dead-letter queue policy and adocumented process for reviewing and reprocessing dead-lettered messages. Poisonmessages MUST NOT block healthy message processing.•Production Service Bus namespaces that need zone or regional redundancy SHALL use thePremium tier, with zone redundancy and Geo-Replication enabled. The design MUSTdocument how and when a secondary region is promoted.

Their roles MUST be assigned at the subscription or resource group scope that theyneed.•Standing RBAC assignments at management group scope for platform teams SHOULD beeligible, not permanent, through Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management with activationlimited to the time needed.•Every RBAC role assignment SHALL follow least privilege, and assignments MUST be made togroups rather than to individual users where practical.•Access to every production subscription MUST be reviewed at least every six months, andassignments that are no longer needed MUST be removed.Naming and tagging•The organization SHALL define and publish one resource naming convention that specifies theordering of components such as resource type, workload, environment, region, and instancenumber. Every Azure resource MUST follow it.•Resource names MUST NOT contain sensitive, personal, or confidential information, becausenames and tags are visible to many services and are not treated as customer data.•Every Azure resource that supports tags MUST carry a defined mandatory tag set that coversat least workload, environment, owner, and cost center. Azure Policy MUST enforce or appendthese tags.•Tag names SHALL use consistent lowercase keys and a controlled vocabulary of values,because tag values are case-sensitive. Tags SHALL NOT hold secrets or sensitive data.Compliance, audit and exceptions•The organization MUST map each applicable regulatory or contractual obligation, such asHIPAA, PCI-DSS, or SOC 2, to specific Azure Policy initiatives or controls, and MUST reviewthe mapping at least annually.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 4 — Network Architecture and EdgeProtectionIntentNetwork controls add defense in depth to identity controls by hiding resources, filtering traffic, andlimiting lateral movement. This chapter requires deliberate segmentation, a well-definedhub-and-spoke or equivalent topology, strict filtering of inbound and outbound flows, and privateconnectivity to platform services. The goal is a small, well-monitored public surface and containedinternal movement.RequirementsTraffic classification and topology•Every production workload SHALL classify each network flow by direction (ingress or egress),scope (north-south or east-west), and visibility (public or private) in its design documentation.•Every Azure landing zone network design SHALL use a documented topology, such ashub-and-spoke or Azure Virtual WAN, with shared connectivity services placed in a dedicatedconnectivity subscription.•Workloads requiring internet exposure SHOULD be placed in subscriptions separate fromworkloads that are reachable only through private or hybrid connectivity.•Every virtual network address space SHALL be allocated from an enterprise IP address planand MUST NOT overlap with any other virtual network or on-premises range that it mayconnect to.Segmentation•Every production workload SHALL be deployed in virtual networks dedicated to that workloador its landing zone, and production and non-production resources MUST NOT share a virtualnetwork.•Every virtual network in a production workload SHALL be divided into subnets by tier or securityrequirement, and each subnet MUST have a network security group attached.•Every network security group SHALL end with a rule that denies all traffic not explicitly allowed,and allow rules MUST specify the narrowest practical source, destination, and port.•Network security group rules MUST NOT allow any-to-any traffic, and inbound rules from theinternet to management ports such as RDP (3389) and SSH (22) SHALL NOT exist.•Virtual network peerings SHALL be created only between networks that have a documentedcommunication need, and forwarded traffic and gateway transit MUST be enabled only wherethe design requires it.•Application security groups or service tags SHOULD be used in network security group rulesinstead of hard-coded IP addresses where the platform supports them.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 14 — AI and Machine Learning WorkloadsIntentAI workloads add risks that conventional applications lack, such as unsafe or ungrounded output,prompt injection, model drift, model retirement and unbounded token spend. This chapter requiresthat safety, data governance, identity, evaluation and cost controls are designed in and verifiedrather than assumed from the hosting platform. It applies to both classic machine learning andgenerative AI workloads.RequirementsArchitecture and layering•The AI workload design MUST define separate layers for client, intelligence (routing,orchestration, agents), inferencing, knowledge (grounding data) and tools, and each layerSHALL enforce its own identity, authorization and caching policy.•The client layer MUST remain thin and SHALL NOT contain model invocation logic, promptcontent, or credentials for model endpoints.•The design MUST route model calls from clients through a back-end gateway (for exampleAzure API Management or an equivalent AI gateway) that enforces authentication, quotas,safety filtering, routing and logging.•The design MUST abstract models and tools behind stable interfaces so that a model orprovider can be replaced without changes to application code.•The architecture document MUST define measurable business success metrics and regulatoryconstraints for the AI capability before the model and platform are selected.Responsible AI and content safety•Every AI workload that produces user-facing content MUST apply input and output contentfiltering (for example Azure AI Content Safety or platform-provided filters), and the team SHALLverify the configured filter levels by testing instead of assuming defaults.•The design MUST include defenses against prompt injection and jailbreak attempts, includingprompt shielding or equivalent controls for both user input and retrieved documents.•The workload MUST set limits on prompt length, output tokens and request rate per identity, sothat abuse cannot cause unbounded consumption.•The team MUST complete and record a responsible AI impact assessment, covering harms,affected groups and mitigations, before any AI feature enters production.•AI features that influence decisions about people SHALL provide human oversight, and thedesign MUST document when a human reviews or can override the output.•The design MUST disclose to users when content is AI-generated and SHOULD provide afeedback channel for reporting harmful or incorrect output.Model, prompt and data governance

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 1 — Reliability and ResiliencyIntentWorkloads fail in ways that cannot be fully predicted, so reliability must be designed in from thestart rather than added after an outage. This chapter requires that availability and recovery targetsare derived from business needs, that redundancy and self-healing are built into critical flows, andthat recovery is rehearsed before it is needed. Meeting these obligations keeps outages short,data loss bounded, and incident response predictable.RequirementsReliability targets•Every production workload SHALL define an availability SLO, an RTO, and an RPO that areagreed in writing with business stakeholders. Targets set without business agreement cannotbe used to justify design cost or to judge whether the design is adequate.•The availability SLO of a production workload MUST reflect the quality promised to its users forthe whole workload, including its dependencies, and MUST NOT be computed solely as thecomposite of dependency SLAs.•Every production workload SHALL define at least one SLI for each availability SLO so thatcompliance with the SLO can be measured continuously.•Reliability targets for a production workload SHOULD be reviewed at least annually and afterevery major incident, and the review outcome MUST be recorded.Flow criticality and failure analysis•Every production workload SHALL identify its user flows and system flows and rate each flowon a documented criticality scale. The ratings drive design investment, test priority, and incidentprioritization.•Every critical flow MUST have its own reliability targets, which MAY be stricter than the targetsof the workload as a whole.•Every production workload SHALL maintain a failure mode analysis that lists each componentand dependency, its possible failure modes, the expected impact, and the planned mitigation.•The failure mode analysis for a production workload MUST be updated whenever a newdependency is added or an architecture change alters a critical flow.Redundancy and zone resilience•Every production workload that has a critical flow SHALL deploy the components serving thatflow redundantly, with no single instance acting as a single point of failure.•Production workloads deployed to an Azure region that offers availability zones SHOULD usezone-redundant or zonal-spread deployments for compute, data, and networking componentsserving critical flows.

rules.sourceContent: •Traffic redirection between regions SHALL be automated through a global routing service, suchas Azure Front Door or Azure Traffic Manager, for workloads whose RTO is shorter than thetime a manual DNS change would take.Backup and restore•Every stateful production data store MUST have automated backups, with a retention periodaligned to the RPO and to regulatory retention requirements, and at least one copy stored in adifferent region or fault domain than the primary.•Backups of production data MUST be protected from deletion and tampering throughimmutability or soft-delete and separate access controls.•Restore procedures for every production data store SHALL be tested at least annually and afterany change to backup configuration or data schema.
