rules.sourceContent: •Every Azure service tier chosen for a production workload MUST have a published SLA whosefigure is at least equal to the availability SLO that the component must support.•Every production workload with a regional-outage RTO shorter than the time needed to rebuildit SHALL be deployed to at least two Azure regions.•Every stateful data store in a production workload SHALL use replication that matches theworkload RPO, and the replication mode (synchronous or asynchronous) MUST bedocumented.Scaling•Every production workload SHALL define a scaling strategy covering the application, data, andinfrastructure tiers, based on measured or forecast usage patterns.•Scaling for production workloads SHOULD be automated through autoscale rules, and manualintervention MUST NOT be required to handle expected load peaks.•Every autoscale configuration SHALL define both scale-out and scale-in rules together withexplicit minimum and maximum instance counts.Self-preservation and self-healing•Every network call from a production workload to a remote dependency SHALL use a timeout,and calls to transient-fault-prone dependencies MUST use retries with exponential back-off andjitter. Unbounded waits and immediate retries amplify outages.•Every production workload that depends on a remote service SHOULD apply a circuit breakerso that repeated failures stop further calls until the dependency recovers.•Every critical flow in a production workload SHOULD define graceful degradation behavior thatpreserves core function when a non-essential dependency is unavailable.•Every load balancer or traffic router fronting a production workload SHALL use health probesthat exercise the dependencies needed by the application, and unhealthy instances MUST beremoved from rotation automatically.•Every message-processing component in a production workload SHALL handle duplicatedelivery safely, so that retried operations are idempotent.Reliability testing•Every production workload SHALL undergo fault-injection or chaos testing against its criticalflows at least annually, and the results MUST be documented with follow-up actions.•Every production workload SHALL be load tested before launch and after any change thatmaterially alters capacity, to confirm that scaling behaves as designed.Backup and disaster recovery•Every production workload SHALL maintain a documented disaster recovery plan coveringevery component and the system as a whole, aligned to the workload RTO and RPO.

patching•Every compute, data, and platform resource in a production workload SHALL be deployed froma hardened configuration that disables unused features, ports, accounts, and services.•Every virtual machine in a production workload SHALL receive operating-system securityupdates through an automated patching process, and critical updates MUST be applied within14 days of release.•Every container image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into theorganization's security operations triage process.•Every security alert rule SHALL have a named owner and MUST be reviewed at least annuallyfor relevance and false-positive rate.•Security log data for production workloads MUST be retained for at least 12 months, or longerwhere a compliance obligation requires it.Security testing and incident response•Every production workload SHALL undergo penetration testing at least annually and aftersignificant architectural change.

The sampling rate SHALL be documented, and sampling decisions MUSTbe consistent across the services in a single transaction.Alerting•Every alert MUST have a named owning team, a severity, and a linked runbook or responseprocedure. Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. Alerting MUST include at least one notification path that is independent of themonitored workload.•Alert rules SHALL be reviewed at least quarterly, and rules that are noisy or never actionableMUST be tuned or removed.SLIs, SLOs and error budgets•Every production service MUST define at least one service-level indicator for availability andone for latency, each with a documented measurement method.•Every production service MUST have a service-level objective for each indicator, agreed withthe service's business owner, with a stated measurement window.•Teams SHOULD track an error budget derived from each objective and MUST define theactions taken, such as pausing feature releases, when the budget is exhausted.Incident response

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 2 — Security Posture and Threat ProtectionIntentSecurity failures expose confidential data, damage integrity, and interrupt service. This chapterrequires a measurable security baseline, classified data, strong encryption, hardenedcomponents, protected secrets, and monitoring and response capability that assume an attackerwill eventually succeed. Layered controls limit the blast radius of any single failure.RequirementsBaseline and secure development•Every production workload SHALL be assessed against a documented security baseline that isaligned with applicable compliance obligations and with Azure platform recommendations.•Every production workload SHALL measure its configuration against the security baseline atleast quarterly, and every deviation MUST be tracked to closure or to a documented, approvedexception.•Every software development team building production workloads SHALL follow a documentedsecure development lifecycle that includes threat modeling during design.•Every build pipeline for a production workload MUST include automated static code analysisand dependency vulnerability scanning, and it SHALL block release when a critical-severityfinding is open.•Every source repository for a production workload SHALL have secret scanning enabled, andcredentials MUST NOT be committed to source control.Data classification and encryption•Every data store and data-processing system in a production workload SHALL be assigned asensitivity classification and an information-type label.•The classification of a data set MUST determine the minimum encryption, retention, and accesscontrols applied to it.•All production data at rest SHALL be encrypted with platform-native encryption usingindustry-standard algorithms.•All production data in transit SHALL be encrypted with TLS 1.2 or later, and plaintext protocolsMUST NOT be used between production components.•Data classified at the highest sensitivity level SHOULD be protected with customer-managedkeys held in Azure Key Vault or Azure Managed HSM.•Every customer-managed encryption key SHALL have a documented rotation schedule andMUST be recoverable through soft delete and purge protection.•Production workloads SHALL NOT disable platform-provided encryption in order to implementcustom cryptography, and custom cryptographic algorithms MUST NOT be created.

rules.sourceContent: •Pipelines MUST run automated build, unit test, static analysis, and dependency vulnerabilityscanning stages before an artifact can be promoted.•A single build artifact MUST be produced once and promoted unchanged through everyenvironment, rather than being rebuilt per environment.•Pipeline identities MUST use least-privilege permissions scoped to the target environment, andSHOULD authenticate to Azure by using workload identity federation instead of storedcredentials.•Production deployments MUST require approval from at least one person other than the authorof the change.Secrets in pipelines•Secrets SHALL NOT be committed to source control, embedded in pipeline definitions, orprinted in pipeline logs. Pipelines MUST retrieve secrets at run time from a secret store such asAzure Key Vault or the pipeline platform's protected secret storage.•Source repositories MUST have secret scanning enabled, and any credential detected in arepository MUST be rotated immediately.•Pipeline service connections and tokens MUST have a defined owner and SHALL be reviewedat least annually.Branching and code review•The default branch of every workload repository MUST be protected so that direct pushes arerejected and changes require a reviewed pull request with passing status checks.•Teams SHOULD use short-lived branches and integrate to the default branch at least daily, sothat changes remain small and incremental.Deployment safety•Every deployment, including code, infrastructure, feature flag, and configuration changes,MUST follow the same standardized, automated process. No category of production changeSHALL be treated as exempt from risk management.•Production releases MUST use progressive exposure, such as canary, blue-green, orring-based rollout, so that a faulty release affects only a subset of users before it is promoted.•A health check MUST pass before a deployment advances to each subsequent stage ofprogressive exposure, and the deployment MUST halt automatically when health checks fail.•Every production deployment MUST have a tested rollback or roll-forward procedure, and theprocedure SHALL be exercised at least annually.•Emergency or hotfix deployments MUST have a documented expedited process that still usesthe pipeline and retains an audit record.Documentation and decision records

rules.sourceContent: •The design MUST test tenant isolation continuously, including automated cross-tenant accesstests in the release pipeline for every production release.•Tenants with stricter isolation or compliance needs SHOULD be offered a dedicateddeployment or dedicated data store, and the document MUST describe how those tenants arerouted to it.•The design MUST document the data residency location of each tenant's data and SHALLensure that tenant data, backups and replicas remain within the region or geography the tenantcontracted for.•The solution MUST support per-tenant encryption key options (for example customer-managedkeys in Azure Key Vault) wherever tenants have contractual requirements for key control, andthe design SHALL document which tiers receive them.•Custom domain handling MUST include a process for removing DNS records when a tenant isoffboarded, so that dangling DNS entries cannot be used for subdomain takeover.Tenant-aware identity and request mapping•The identity design MUST map every authenticated request to exactly one tenant by using averifiable claim in the token, a trusted lookup, or another documented mechanism, and MUSTNOT derive the tenant from an unvalidated client-supplied value.•The architecture document MUST state how tenant context is propagated across services,queues and background jobs, so that downstream components enforce the same tenantboundary.•The design SHALL apply least privilege and zero trust principles to tenant administrators, andtenant-level roles MUST NOT grant access to platform-level management operations.•Operator and support access to tenant data MUST be limited to approved, time-bound andlogged sessions.Noisy neighbour and fairness•The design MUST include resource governance that prevents a single tenant from exhaustingshared capacity, using per-tenant quotas, rate limits or throttling that return a defined error tothe caller.•The platform MUST monitor resource consumption per tenant as well as in aggregate, andSHALL alert on per-tenant usage spikes before shared capacity is exhausted.•The design SHOULD offer higher-isolation tiers (reserved throughput, premium service tiers ordedicated instances) for tenants whose workload would otherwise threaten shared capacity.•The team MUST define service-level objectives for the solution based on tenant requirementsand SHALL load-test the solution at the projected maximum tenant count and at the projectedpeak load of its largest tenant.Tenant lifecycle, metering and operations

rules.sourceContent: •The team MUST record the source, version, licence terms and intended use of every model in amodel inventory and MUST confirm that the licence permits the intended commercial use.•The workload MUST keep prompts, system messages and model configuration in versioncontrol and SHALL deploy them through a controlled release process, so that telemetry can becorrelated with a specific prompt version.•The design MUST plan for model deprecation by recording the retirement date of each hostedmodel version and by providing a tested fallback model or migration path before that date.•Training, fine-tuning and grounding data MUST have a documented owner, classification,lineage and retention period, and personal or confidential data SHALL NOT be used for trainingunless the legal basis is recorded.•Retrieval over grounding data MUST enforce the end user's authorization, by passing user ortenant identity to the retrieval layer so results are security-trimmed, and AI components MUSTNOT read data stores directly.Evaluation and monitoring•The team MUST evaluate each model and prompt change against a versioned test dataset forgroundedness, relevance, safety and accuracy before release, and SHALL block release whenresults fall below defined thresholds.•The workload MUST include red-team or adversarial testing of the AI feature before initialproduction release and after any change of model, grounding source or system prompt.•The production workload MUST monitor model quality indicators (accuracy drift, inferencelatency, confidence scores and input data distribution) and SHALL alert when a definedthreshold is breached.•The workload MUST log prompts, completions and tool calls with user identity and promptversion for audit, and the log retention and redaction rules SHALL be documented for anypersonal data they contain.Identity, secrets and network•Services calling Azure OpenAI, Azure AI services or Azure Machine Learning endpoints MUSTauthenticate with managed identities or Microsoft Entra ID, and API keys MUST NOT beembedded in code or configuration files.•Where API keys cannot be avoided, the workload MUST store them in Azure Key Vault andSHALL rotate them at least every 90 days.•Production AI endpoints and grounding data stores SHOULD be reachable only through privateendpoints, and public network access MUST be disabled unless a documented exceptionexists.•Agents and tools MUST run with the least-privilege identity needed for their actions, and anytool that changes state SHALL require explicit authorization checks independent of the model'soutput.Cost and capacity

The sampling rate SHALL be documented, and sampling decisions MUSTbe consistent across the services in a single transaction.Alerting•Every alert MUST have a named owning team, a severity, and a linked runbook or responseprocedure. Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. Alerting MUST include at least one notification path that is independent of themonitored workload.•Alert rules SHALL be reviewed at least quarterly, and rules that are noisy or never actionableMUST be tuned or removed.SLIs, SLOs and error budgets•Every production service MUST define at least one service-level indicator for availability andone for latency, each with a documented measurement method.•Every production service MUST have a service-level objective for each indicator, agreed withthe service's business owner, with a stated measurement window.•Teams SHOULD track an error budget derived from each objective and MUST define theactions taken, such as pausing feature releases, when the budget is exhausted.Incident response

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 12 — Disaster Recovery, BusinessContinuity and Performance EfficiencyIntentRecovery targets, tested failover, and measured performance determine whether a workloadmeets its commitments when conditions are bad. Untested backups and untested scalingassumptions fail at the worst moment. This chapter sets obligations for recovery objectives,multi-region design, restore and failover testing, load testing, capacity planning, and caching.RequirementsRecovery objectives and planning•Every production workload SHALL be assigned a business criticality tier, and every tier MUSThave documented RTO and RPO targets. Components with different criticality inside oneworkload MUST each have their own recovery approach documented.•Every production workload MUST have a written disaster recovery plan covering allcomponents and the system as a whole, with explicit activation criteria that distinguish adisaster from a minor incident.•The disaster recovery plan MUST name owners for declaring a disaster, executing recovery,communicating with stakeholders, and closing the incident, and it SHALL define escalationpaths and prepared communication channels.•The disaster recovery plan MUST be reviewed and updated at least annually and after everyarchitecture change that affects recovery.Multi-region design and data replication•Each workload's design document MUST state the recovery pattern chosen, such asactive-active, active-passive warm standby, or active-passive cold standby, and show that thepattern can meet the documented RTO.•The secondary region of every multi-region production workload MUST have its networktopology, identity configuration, and deployment automation prepared before a disaster, so thatrecovery does not depend on building them during the event.•Data replication mode SHALL follow RPO targets, with synchronous replication used wherezero data loss is required and asynchronous replication accepted only where the RPO toleratesthe lag. Replication lag MUST be monitored and alerted.•Workloads SHOULD be isolated into components that can be failed over independently, andeach partial-failover path MUST be documented and tested separately.•Failback to the primary region MUST be planned and documented as a separate procedurefrom failover.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 15 — Sustainability and Efficient ResourceUseIntentEvery design decision affects how much compute, storage and network a workload consumes,and idle or oversized resources waste energy and money alike. Sustainability depends onremoving waste, measuring emissions and assigning ownership, without undermining reliability,security or performance. This chapter turns those practices into obligations for design andoperations.RequirementsGovernance and measurement•Every production workload MUST have a named owner accountable for resource efficiency andsustainability targets, and the owner SHALL be recorded in the workload documentation.•The workload team MUST define at least one measurable efficiency or emissions target (forexample average CPU utilization, carbon per transaction or monthly emissions) and SHALLreview it at least quarterly.•The team SHOULD measure workload emissions by using Azure carbon optimization or anequivalent tool, and MUST record the baseline and each reported change.•The architecture document MUST record the sustainability trade-offs of reliability, performanceand security decisions, such as multiregion duplication, extra caching or long telemetryretention.Right-sizing and utilization•The team MUST right-size every production compute resource against measured utilization atleast every six months, and SHALL document the observed utilization used as evidence.•The design MUST define a target average utilization for each compute tier and SHALL justifyany tier running persistently below that target.•Stateless and variable-load components MUST use autoscaling (for example virtual machinescale sets, Azure Kubernetes Service autoscalers or App Service autoscale) with a definedminimum and maximum instance count, instead of being sized for peak demand.•Non-production environments MUST shut down or scale to zero outside documented workinghours, unless the document records a reason for continuous operation.•The team MUST identify and remove idle or orphaned resources (unattached disks, unusedpublic IP addresses, empty clusters and unused snapshots) at least monthly, and SHOULDautomate the detection.•The design SHOULD prefer managed PaaS or serverless services over self-managed virtualmachines where they meet requirements, because shared platform capacity is used moreefficiently.

rules.sourceContent: Chapter 10 — Services, APIs and MessagingIntentServices communicate over networks that fail, throttle, and deliver messages more than once.Well-designed APIs, bounded retries, and durable messaging keep one component's failure fromcascading and let producers and consumers evolve independently. This chapter sets obligationsfor API design and versioning, service-to-service calls, and asynchronous messaging on Azure.RequirementsAPI design•Every web API SHALL model its URIs on resources named with nouns, and collection URIsMUST use plural nouns. Verbs such as `create-order` SHALL NOT appear in resource URIs.•Every web API MUST use HTTP methods according to their standard semantics and MUSTreturn accurate HTTP status codes, such as 201 with a Location header for creation and 404for missing resources.•GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD, and PATCH operations of every web API MUST be idempotent. Arepeated request against the same resource must leave the resource in the same state.•A POST operation that creates a resource MUST NOT cause side effects on resourcesunrelated to the new resource.•Every web API operation that takes long to complete SHOULD return HTTP 202 with a statusendpoint URI in the Location header, instead of holding the client connection open.•Every web API collection endpoint MUST support pagination with documented default andmaximum page sizes. The maximum limit prevents a single request from retrieving unboundeddata.•Web APIs SHOULD support content negotiation through the Accept header and MUST return415 for unsupported request media types and 406 when no acceptable response format exists.•Every public API MUST publish a machine-readable contract, such as an OpenAPI document,that is kept in source control with the implementation.API versioning and gateway•Every API consumed outside its owning team MUST carry an explicit version in the URI, aheader, or a query parameter. Unversioned public endpoints SHALL NOT be released.•A breaking change to an API contract, such as removing a field, changing a type, or changingrequired parameters, SHALL be released only as a new major version. The existing majorversion MUST remain available during a published deprecation period.•Every API version retirement MUST be announced to consumers in advance, with a stated enddate, before the version is removed.

rules.sourceContent: •Every API exposed to external or cross-team consumers SHALL be published through an APIgateway, such as Azure API Management, rather than directly from the backend service. Thegateway applies authentication, rate limiting, and policy consistently.•API gateway policies for every production API MUST enforce request rate limits or quotas andMUST validate inbound requests against the published contract.Service-to-service communication•Every outbound call to a remote service or dependency MUST have an explicit timeout. Callswithout timeouts SHALL NOT be shipped, because blocked threads and connections canexhaust resources.•Every retry policy MUST apply only to transient faults, use exponential backoff with jitter, andenforce a maximum attempt count. Retries for non-transient errors SHALL NOT be attempted.•Retry logic SHALL be implemented at only one layer of a call chain. Lower layers MUST failfast so that nested retries do not multiply delays and load.•Every dependency call that can fail persistently MUST be wrapped by a circuit breaker withdocumented failure threshold, open duration, and half-open probe behavior. Retry logic MUSTstop when the circuit breaker reports the circuit is open.•Retried operations that are not naturally idempotent MUST carry an idempotency key orrequest identifier that the receiving service uses to discard duplicates.•Early retry failures SHOULD be logged as informational entries and the final exhausted retryMUST be logged as an error, so that operators are not flooded with alerts for recovered faults.•Each service MUST own its data store, and other services SHALL access that data onlythrough the owning service's API or published events. Shared databases betweenindependently deployed services SHALL NOT be used.•Service boundaries SHOULD align with business capabilities, and each service MUST beindependently deployable and versionable.•Application code SHOULD use the official Azure SDK client libraries and their built-in retry andauthentication support instead of hand-built REST calls to Azure services.Messaging•Every messaging consumer MUST be idempotent, because Azure Service Bus and AzureEvent Grid deliver at least once. Consumers SHOULD track processed message identifiers todetect duplicates.•Every Service Bus queue and subscription SHALL have a dead-letter queue policy and adocumented process for reviewing and reprocessing dead-lettered messages. Poisonmessages MUST NOT block healthy message processing.•Production Service Bus namespaces that need zone or regional redundancy SHALL use thePremium tier, with zone redundancy and Geo-Replication enabled. The design MUSTdocument how and when a secondary region is promoted.

Retries for non-transient errors SHALL NOT be attempted.•Retry logic SHALL be implemented at only one layer of a call chain. Consumers SHOULD track processed message identifiers todetect duplicates.•Every Service Bus queue and subscription SHALL have a dead-letter queue policy and adocumented process for reviewing and reprocessing dead-lettered messages. Poisonmessages MUST NOT block healthy message processing.•Production Service Bus namespaces that need zone or regional redundancy SHALL use thePremium tier, with zone redundancy and Geo-Replication enabled. rules.sourceContent: Chapter 13 — Multitenancy and SaaS ArchitectureIntentA multitenant solution serves several customers from shared components, so a weakness inisolation, fairness or tenant identification affects every customer at once. This chapter setsobligations for defining tenants, choosing tenancy models, keeping tenant data separate,controlling noisy neighbours, and automating the tenant lifecycle. Following it lets a provider scaletenants without trading away security, reliability or cost transparency.RequirementsTenant definition and tenancy model•The solution architecture document MUST define what a tenant is for the solution (for examplea customer organization, a customer division, or a consumer group) and MUST state howtenants differ from individual users. An unclear tenant definition leads to inconsistent isolationand billing boundaries.•The architecture document MUST state the expected number of tenants at launch and theplanned growth, and the tenancy model MUST be justified against that projection.•The architecture document MUST record, for each solution component (compute, data,messaging, identity), the selected tenancy model (shared, sharded or dedicated per tenant)together with the isolation, cost and compliance reasons for the choice.•The architecture document SHALL document the tenancy-model decision as an architecturedecision record that lists business objectives, compliance needs, scale, automation capacityand SLA expectations as decision inputs.•Where a design deploys dedicated Azure resources per tenant, the design SHOULD placeeach tenant in its own Azure subscription or SHALL document how subscription quotas andlimits are managed as the tenant count grows.•The architecture document MUST distinguish logical tenants from physical deployments whenmore than one tenant can share a deployment, and MUST describe how tenants are mapped todeployments.Tenant isolation and data protection•The design MUST include a documented tenant isolation model that identifies, for every sharedcomponent, how one tenant is prevented from reading or modifying another tenant's data.•Application code and data-access layers MUST apply the tenant identifier as a mandatory filteror partition key on every query against shared data stores. Row-level security, per-tenantschemas, per-tenant databases or equivalent controls SHALL back the application-level filterwhere the data store supports them.•The design MUST NOT allow any request to reach tenant data without a resolved andauthorized tenant context.

This chapter setsobligations for defining tenants, choosing tenancy models, keeping tenant data separate,controlling noisy neighbours, and automating the tenant lifecycle. Following it lets a provider scaletenants without trading away security, reliability or cost transparency.RequirementsTenant definition and tenancy model•The solution architecture document MUST define what a tenant is for the solution (for examplea customer organization, a customer division, or a consumer group) and MUST state howtenants differ from individual users. An unclear tenant definition leads to inconsistent isolationand billing boundaries.•The architecture document MUST state the expected number of tenants at launch and theplanned growth, and the tenancy model MUST be justified against that projection.•The architecture document MUST record, for each solution component (compute, data,messaging, identity), the selected tenancy model (shared, sharded or dedicated per tenant)together with the isolation, cost and compliance reasons for the choice.•The architecture document SHALL document the tenancy-model decision as an architecturedecision record that lists business objectives, compliance needs, scale, automation capacityand SLA expectations as decision inputs.•Where a design deploys dedicated Azure resources per tenant, the design SHOULD placeeach tenant in its own Azure subscription or SHALL document how subscription quotas andlimits are managed as the tenant count grows.•The architecture document MUST distinguish logical tenants from physical deployments whenmore than one tenant can share a deployment, and MUST describe how tenants are mapped todeployments.Tenant isolation and data protection•The design MUST include a documented tenant isolation model that identifies, for every sharedcomponent, how one tenant is prevented from reading or modifying another tenant's data.•Application code and data-access layers MUST apply the tenant identifier as a mandatory filteror partition key on every query against shared data stores. Row-level security, per-tenantschemas, per-tenant databases or equivalent controls SHALL back the application-level filterwhere the data store supports them.•The design MUST NOT allow any request to reach tenant data without a resolved andauthorized tenant context.

positive: The design maps each tenant to a deployment group and documents reassignment during scaling.
negative: The document describes source-code branching and release notes.

rules.remediation: Explicitly distinguish logical tenant entities from physical deployments in shared deployments.

rules.sourceContent: •The design MUST test tenant isolation continuously, including automated cross-tenant accesstests in the release pipeline for every production release.•Tenants with stricter isolation or compliance needs SHOULD be offered a dedicateddeployment or dedicated data store, and the document MUST describe how those tenants arerouted to it.•The design MUST document the data residency location of each tenant's data and SHALLensure that tenant data, backups and replicas remain within the region or geography the tenantcontracted for.•The solution MUST support per-tenant encryption key options (for example customer-managedkeys in Azure Key Vault) wherever tenants have contractual requirements for key control, andthe design SHALL document which tiers receive them.•Custom domain handling MUST include a process for removing DNS records when a tenant isoffboarded, so that dangling DNS entries cannot be used for subdomain takeover.Tenant-aware identity and request mapping•The identity design MUST map every authenticated request to exactly one tenant by using averifiable claim in the token, a trusted lookup, or another documented mechanism, and MUSTNOT derive the tenant from an unvalidated client-supplied value.•The architecture document MUST state how tenant context is propagated across services,queues and background jobs, so that downstream components enforce the same tenantboundary.•The design SHALL apply least privilege and zero trust principles to tenant administrators, andtenant-level roles MUST NOT grant access to platform-level management operations.•Operator and support access to tenant data MUST be limited to approved, time-bound andlogged sessions.Noisy neighbour and fairness•The design MUST include resource governance that prevents a single tenant from exhaustingshared capacity, using per-tenant quotas, rate limits or throttling that return a defined error tothe caller.•The platform MUST monitor resource consumption per tenant as well as in aggregate, andSHALL alert on per-tenant usage spikes before shared capacity is exhausted.•The design SHOULD offer higher-isolation tiers (reserved throughput, premium service tiers ordedicated instances) for tenants whose workload would otherwise threaten shared capacity.•The team MUST define service-level objectives for the solution based on tenant requirementsand SHALL load-test the solution at the projected maximum tenant count and at the projectedpeak load of its largest tenant.Tenant lifecycle, metering and operations

image deployed to production SHALL be built from an approved base imageand scanned for vulnerabilities, and images with unremediated critical vulnerabilities MUSTNOT be deployed.•Every production Azure subscription SHOULD have Microsoft Defender for Cloud enabled withits recommendations triaged at least monthly.Secrets management•Every application secret in a production workload SHALL be stored in a dedicated secret storesuch as Azure Key Vault, and secrets MUST NOT be stored in source code, container images,or plain-text configuration files.•Every production workload SHOULD use managed identities in place of stored credentialswherever the target service supports them.•Every production secret SHALL have a defined rotation interval, and the secret managementprocess MUST support emergency rotation outside the schedule.•Every consumer of a preshared key SHALL receive its own distinct key, and the same keyMUST NOT be used in both production and non-production environments.•Every access to production secrets and every change to them SHALL be written to an audit logthat is retained and monitored.Threat detection and monitoring•Every production workload SHALL forward security-relevant logs from compute, identity,network, and data tiers to a central security log store.•Every production workload SHALL have threat detection enabled that raises alerts into rules.sourceContent: •Workspace-based Application Insights resources SHOULD be used so that application andinfrastructure telemetry can be queried together.•Access to log workspaces MUST be controlled by role-based access control, and workspacesholding security or audit data SHALL be restricted to authorized personnel.Retention•The retention period for each log category MUST be defined in the design document andSHALL satisfy the longest applicable regulatory or organizational requirement.•Audit and security logs SHOULD be kept for at least one year, using archive or long-termstorage tiers for the period beyond interactive retention to control cost.•Log data MUST be protected from alteration and deletion for the duration of its retention period.Distributed tracing and sampling•Every request that crosses a service boundary MUST propagate a correlation identifier, usingthe W3C Trace Context standard, so that a transaction can be traced end to end.•Services in a distributed system SHALL emit trace spans for all inbound requests and outbounddependency calls.•Sampling, when used for traces or telemetry in production, MUST preserve all failed requestsand all exceptions. The sampling rate SHALL be documented, and sampling decisions MUSTbe consistent across the services in a single transaction.Alerting•Every alert MUST have a named owning team, a severity, and a linked runbook or responseprocedure. Alerts without an owner SHALL NOT be enabled in production.•Alerts MUST be based on symptoms that affect users or on breach of a service-level objective,and SHOULD NOT fire on causes that require no human action.•Production alert rules and action groups MUST be defined as code and stored in versioncontrol. Alerting MUST include at least one notification path that is independent of themonitored workload.•Alert rules SHALL be reviewed at least quarterly, and rules that are noisy or never actionableMUST be tuned or removed.SLIs, SLOs and error budgets•Every production service MUST define at least one service-level indicator for availability andone for latency, each with a documented measurement method.•Every production service MUST have a service-level objective for each indicator, agreed withthe service's business owner, with a stated measurement window.•Teams SHOULD track an error budget derived from each objective and MUST define theactions taken, such as pausing feature releases, when the budget is exhausted.Incident response
